item.title: Staff Post - Wikiwalk Proposal
item.content:encoded:
Timer Expired. Edits made as discussed below. Author may revert at any time.

The WikiWalk team is proposing edits to this page. All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 7 days if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team

+ Show Block
- Hide Block

Alright. So there are two crosslinks I'm going to propose here. The first is a crosslink to SCP-423, since its likely the SCP Foundation may see if the beetles consider his presence in a work as an error or not, testing their abilities. Additionally, the tale Memory makes use of the beetles as part of a larger experiment, and an in-line link there would not go amiss, maybe. As such, I am recommending the following edits:

Changing this:

A single individual from the 14-member colony that comprises SCP-410 may be removed for research and functional application for a single two (2) hour activity period daily with approval from the senior researcher on duty. No more than four (4) members of the colony are to be removed at any given time. Transport of a single SCP-410 colony member should be facilitated by no fewer than two (2) Class 2 entomology staff using only an approved SCP-410 transport module to do so. The current SCP-410 transport modules are 20 x 20 x 20cm transparent acrylic glass containers perforated with twelve (12) 1mm ventilation holes and each featuring a hinged lid equipped with a simple latch.

To this:

A single individual from the 14-member colony that comprises SCP-410 may be removed for research and functional application for a single two (2) hour activity period daily with approval from the senior researcher on duty. No more than four (4) members of the colony are to be removed at any given time. Transport of a single SCP-410 colony member should be facilitated by no fewer than two (2) Class 2 entomology staff using only an approved SCP-410 transport module to do so. The current SCP-410 transport modules are 20 x 20 x 20cm transparent acrylic glass containers perforated with twelve (12) 1mm ventilation holes and each featuring a hinged lid equipped with a simple latch.

Adding the following paragraph below the list of edited materials:

Proposed testing of SCP-410 with anomalous texts, including texts containing SCP-423, is currently pending review.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The only issue I have with this article is the dialogue. For instance:

"I know you're busy, Professor, but this grant is due in 45 minutes. I need to use them."

That wording is painfully contrived. The student knows the bug thing is weird and the professor most likely made it a point to keep it secret from most people. So why would a student be so stupid as to discuss this clearly strange-ass object that allows you to cheat, no less, in front of a complete stranger? Instead, it would be a little more organic to say that the student steps in the classroom and waits by the door with an anxious expression on his or her face, a document in his or her hand, trying to gain the attention of the teacher without interrupting the conversation. The teacher nods the student over, the student mutters something like, "it's due in 45 minutes," the teacher takes the paper and puts it into the box. In the process of opening it, the Foundation member notices movement inside the box, like an insect, and inquires about it. It is at this point that the teacher becomes hostile and the Foundation member becomes extremely suspicious, and so on…

Turning that idea into a couple of clinical Foundation sentences would help the article a ton.

"I didn't sign up for no bugs, you bastards!"

I know the guy is an oaf, but come on. It's not necessary to add excerpts of this guy's stupid dialogue as it's a test log, not an interview. The compelling aspect of a test log is what happens as a result of testing something. Adding little comic asides doesn't help our understanding of the situation, and it kills the clinical tone of the article.

Other than that, I think it's one of the better articles that I've read on this site because, other than the weird dialogue choices, it really nails that "government document" tone better than a lot of the other articles.
